d: Perceptive faculty.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: Sense refers to a capacity for perception or awareness. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at Hebrews 5:14, and names a sense rather than an action, person, or place. The surrounding verse text is not included, so its specific force there cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is a means of perceiving or recognizing something in ordinary use.

d: From another place, by another way.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means "elsewhere," "from another way," or "from elsewhere." It points to a different place or direction rather than the one currently being discussed. As an adverb, it describes where something comes from or where it is found, helping distinguish one location or route from another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in Mark 1:38 and John 10:1. Its precise force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains movement or location associated with somewhere different.

d: To refresh, revive, comfort.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “refreshed” or “to refresh”: to bring renewed strength, relief, or encouragement to someone. It describes a restoring effect rather than merely providing information or giving instruction. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Timothy 1:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains clear: someone’s weariness or burden is eased, and renewed strength or comfort is received.

Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: A star.

e.t: This word means “stars,” referring to the visible lights in the sky. It is used of individual stars as well as stars considered together. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Luke, Acts, and Hebrews. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a star is a heavenly light, while stars are the many such lights seen together. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is describing ordinary observation, a sign, or a comparison, but the word itself names stars.

d: A queen.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “queen”: a woman recognized as the female ruler or royal consort of a kingdom. It is a noun that names a person rather than an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Revelation. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding context.

d: To cause to gush forth, send forth.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to flow” or “to pour,” describing liquid coming out or moving onward. It is used only once in the Greek New Testament, in James 3:11. The image concerns what comes from a source, making the word useful for describing the character of what emerges from something. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context and the comparison being made there.

d: In the Hebrew, or rather, in the Aramaic dialect.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “in Aramaic,” identifying the language being used or referred to. It functions as a language description rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing in John and Revelation. Its use marks words, names, or expressions as Aramaic, while the exact significance of that language reference depends on the surrounding verse. The word itself points simply to Aramaic as the language connected with the statement or name.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “one,” referring to a single person, thing, or unit rather than two or more. It can identify an individual, emphasize singularity, or express that something is one in number. The same basic meaning appears throughout the New Testament, where the word occurs 345 times in 288 verses. Its exact grammatical role depends on the sentence, but its central idea remains singularity: one person, one thing, or one unified whole.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means to sneak in or to worm one’s way into a place or situation, emphasizing quiet, gradual, or concealed entry. It describes the manner of entering rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 3:6. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is an unobtrusive entry.

d: Working, action, productive work, activity; in the NT, confined to superhuman activity.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word describes active energy at work—the effective operation or working of power. It can refer to power actively producing a result, especially God’s power working in people, in the body of Christ, or in the transformation of believers. Its central idea is not merely strength possessed, but strength operating and accomplishing something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, and it is consistently rendered “working.” The surrounding passage determines whose power is operating and what result that power produces.

d: Inquiry, request, appeal, demand; a profession, pledge.

e.t: This word means “pledge”: a solemn promise or commitment made by someone. It refers to an expressed assurance that binds a person to what has been promised, rather than merely describing a feeling or intention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 3:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a pledge or committed response.

d: A little young goat.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: This word means “a goat,” referring to the animal. It is used once in the Greek New Testament, at Matthew 25:33. The plural rendering “goats” reflects how the word appears in that verse, but its basic lexical meaning remains goat. Understanding the word identifies the kind of animal being named; the particular significance it carries in Matthew depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: (a) comely, seemly, decorous, (b) of honorable position (in society), wealthy, influential.

e.t: This word describes something as “presentable” or “proper”—fitting, respectable, and suitable in appearance or conduct. It can describe a person, an arrangement, or something that is considered appropriate rather than disorderly or unbecoming. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Mark, Acts, and 1 Corinthians. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as fitting or presentable.

d: Rule, authority, sovereignty; a reign.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “reign”: the period during which a ruler governs. It focuses on the ruler’s governing era or dominion rather than naming the ruler himself. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 3:1. Its specific reference there depends on the surrounding historical statement, but the central idea remains the exercise of rule during a defined period. The word therefore describes a ruler’s time of governing and the authority associated with that rule.

d: Age, term of life; full age, maturity; stature.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to a person’s age or stage of life, and in some contexts to physical height. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on age, the length of life, or bodily stature. The same word can therefore describe how long someone has lived or how tall someone is. It occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, making it uncommon but used across several Gospel and letter passages.

me: Adjective, Dative, Plural, Masculine, Person Gentilic

e.t: “Jewish” refers to something connected with the Jewish people, their identity, or their customs. It functions as an adjective, describing a matter as belonging to or associated with Jews rather than naming a separate action or object. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Titus 1:14. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains “Jewish.”

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, showing use in several settings while retaining this central idea of lowering or taking something down. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being taken down and the surrounding sentence.

As a verb, its exact English wording depends on whether the sentence emphasizes being placed or being appointed. It occurs 24 times in the Greek New Testament, including uses across the Gospels and Revelation.

It is a verb used in the Greek New Testament, including passages where people are urged to knock persistently and where someone stands at a door and knocks. The word occurs nine times in nine New Testament verses, with occurrences in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Revelation.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: “Especially” marks one person, group, or matter as receiving particular emphasis within a broader statement. It draws attention to something included in what has already been said, showing that it deserves focused consideration. This word functions as an adverb, shaping how the surrounding action or statement should be understood rather than naming a person or thing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times, consistently adding this kind of emphasis.

The word appears six times in the Greek New Testament, in Acts, Galatians, Hebrews, and Jude. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being changed or moved and how the surrounding sentence presents that action.

In the New Testament, it is used six times, chiefly in 2 Corinthians and once in Philippians. Its usual English renderings are “minds” and “thought,” showing that it can refer either to people’s inward understanding or to the thoughts occupying them. The surrounding verse determines its precise emphasis.

The wording may appear as “building” or “builds” when the sentence requires it.

Its basic meaning remains consistent across these uses, while the exact role it plays in a particular sentence is determined by the surrounding context.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times: once in Ephesians, once in 2 Timothy, and four times in Hebrews. Its use therefore covers discipline in both family and spiritual instruction settings, while its central meaning remains the same: purposeful discipline that forms and corrects. The surrounding verse determines the particular emphasis in each occurrence.

d: A transgression, violation of law.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “lawlessness” or “wrongdoing.” It describes conduct that disregards or violates what is lawful, expressing moral failure rather than a mere mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:16. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains behavior that opposes lawful or right conduct.

d: Dwelling around; a neighbor.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “neighboring,” describing people or places located nearby. It points to those who live in the surrounding area rather than to people far away. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 1:58. The word itself gives a general description of nearness; the surrounding verse determines exactly whom it identifies in that passage. Its central idea is simple: those close by, in the neighboring area.

It can express an object, purpose, goal, or situation that is put before people as something to consider or pursue. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in 2 Corinthians, Hebrews, and Jude. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being placed before the reader or hearer.

d: Approach, access, admission.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “access”—the ability to approach or enter into someone’s presence. In the New Testament, it describes the believer’s welcome into God’s presence and the resulting confidence to draw near. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Romans and twice in Ephesians. Its repeated use in these letters connects access with the standing believers have through Christ, though the precise emphasis in each verse comes from its surrounding context.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, both in Luke, so its meaning is clear but its use is limited. The surrounding passage determines whether the word emphasizes the person who is frightened or the effect that produces fear. Its two recorded uses appear in Luke 21:9 and Luke 24:37.

The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in Luke, Acts, Philippians, and 1 Peter. In each occurrence, the surrounding verse determines whether the word points to a physical description or carries a broader descriptive force. Its repeated English rendering as “crooked” supports this basic meaning.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in the Gospels, and its meaning remains centered on accompanying others. The surrounding verse determines who is going together and why, but the word itself emphasizes joining someone’s journey or proceeding alongside them.

Its basic sense emphasizes agreement between people, while the surrounding context determines whether that agreement is simply joining together or specifically joining others in an accusation.

e.t: Syntyche is a personal name, referring to a woman named Syntyche. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Philippians 4:2, and the English translations retain it as “Syntyche.” The surrounding verse is needed to explain her specific role in that passage; the name itself identifies the person.

d: Dark purple or blue, of the color of hyacinth.

e.t: This word describes something dark blue in color. It is a color term, pointing to a deep or richly shaded blue rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 9:17. The precise significance of the color in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself gives a straightforward visual description: dark blue.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, so its basic sense appears across several settings without becoming a specialized term. The surrounding verse determines what is being shown and how the action functions there.

d: Peleg, son of Eber, and one of the ancestors of Jesus.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Peleg is a personal name identifying a person, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, rendered “Peleg,” at Luke 3:35. Because the available material provides the name but not the surrounding verse text, its significance in that particular passage cannot be described further here. Its ordinary lexical role is simply to identify Peleg as an individual named in the New Testament record.

d: A debtor.
me: Noun, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “debtor”: a person who owes money or some other obligation to another. It describes people viewed in relation to what they are required to repay, rather than focusing on the lender or the debt itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains someone who is obligated because something is owed.

d: (a) a pebble, small stone, (b) hence, from their use in voting: a vote.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means a stone, and it can also refer to a small stone used as a vote or ballot. Its basic sense is a physical stone, while its voting sense describes how such an object could express a decision. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times across two verses, including Acts 26:10 and Revelation 2:17. The exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.
